headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors from Kestra workflows feeding LangChain4j, with medium data-leakage and compliance exposure from shared automation surfaces.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Kestra can ingest files, logs, messages, and stdin/stdout, and LangChain4j is a framework for LLM apps that may consume those outputs. A shared filesystem or message bridge is plausible, so attacker-controlled workflow content could be treated as instructions. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Kestra workflow outputs are passed into LangChain4j prompts or tools without sanitization
IF both agents share /app/storage, /tmp, or another message channel
mitigations: Add a strict delimiter and instruction/data separation in prompts
Disable automatic ingestion of workflow logs into LLM prompts
Require provenance tags on all Kestra outputs before reuse
Review shared filesystem mounts and remove unnecessary bridges
requires-engineering: add content filtering or prompt-firewall middleware

B_data_leakage.rationale: Kestra touches logs, inputs, artifacts, database data, cloud storage data, messages, and notifications, while LangChain4j is a general LLM framework that may forward context to model backends. If the pair shares a workspace or passes sensitive workflow data into LLM calls, leakage can occur in default automation flows. The evidence is indirect, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF sensitive Kestra artifacts or logs are inserted into LangChain4j prompts
IF LangChain4j is configured to call a third-party model backend with that context
mitigations: Minimize sensitive fields in Kestra outputs
Mask secrets before any LLM handoff
Restrict shared directories to non-sensitive artifacts
Audit prompt templates for accidental log inclusion
requires-engineering: enforce DLP/redaction at the orchestration boundary

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Kestra has broad filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and network egress capabilities, and it requests elevated privileges including root and docker.sock. LangChain4j itself is a library, but when paired in the same automation environment it can drive overlapping mutable resources through the host application. Because both can participate in the same mutable workflow stack and no locking is documented, conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, database, or queue
IF the host application lets LangChain4j-triggered actions modify resources Kestra also mutates
mitigations: Separate writable directories per agent
Serialize writes with a lock or queue
Disable unnecessary root or docker.sock access
Use per-agent service accounts and credentials
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency or transactional coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: Kestra can emit workflow outputs, logs, notifications, and downstream actions, while LangChain4j is commonly used to turn model output into application behavior. If LangChain4j consumes Kestra output as authoritative, a bad workflow result can cascade into incorrect messages or actions. The pair has no documented verification step, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF LangChain4j uses Kestra-generated text as a source of truth
IF downstream actions are triggered from that text without human or rule-based verification
mitigations: Add validation before any action-taking step
Require human approval for high-impact outputs
Compare Kestra outputs against independent checks
Log and flag low-confidence model-derived decisions
requires-engineering: implement schema validation and provenance checks

E_compliance.rationale: Kestra processes logs, inputs, artifacts, database data, cloud storage data, messages, and notifications, which can include regulated data classes. LangChain4j is a general LLM framework with unspecified residency, retention, and model-backend handling in this profile. Because the pair could route regulated data into an unverified LLM path, compliance risk is medium, not low.
conditions: IF regulated data from Kestra is sent through LangChain4j to a non-approved backend
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the workflow data
mitigations: Classify data before any LLM call
Block regulated fields from prompt construction
Document approved backends and regions
Set short retention on workflow logs
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
